summary: This document describes JSON data structures that represent registration information held by Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries. They form the responses of RDAP queries. It obsoletes RFC 7483.

plainLanguage.summary: The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) returns registration information about names, people, and Internet number resources. This RFC defines a shared JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) layout so clients can read answers consistently.

questions: what does an rdap response look like
what format do rdap responses use
subtitle: A shared JSON format for registry answers about domains, nameservers, people, IP networks, and AS numbers.

tldr.problem: Clients querying registration services need a consistent way to interpret data from Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9083 defines shared JSON types and structures, five registration object classes, search and error responses, and ways to indicate incomplete results.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9083 is Internet Standard STD 95 and obsoletes RFC 7483. It is the current response-format specification in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 9083 is Internet Standard STD 95 and it obsoletes RFC 7483. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What RDAP Responses Contain
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) provides access to registration data held by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and Domain Name Registries (DNRs). RFC 9082 defines query formats; RFC 7480 describes HTTP use. RFC 9083 defines the JSON response bodies.

A response may describe one object or contain an array of matching objects from a search. The shared model covers domains, nameservers, and entities for both registry types. RIRs also return IP network and Autonomous System number objects.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the layout of RDAP answers. A lookup returns one record, while a search returns a list of records.

sections.title: JSON Names and Extensions
sections.content:
JSON member names are case sensitive, and servers and clients must use the specified spelling. Clients should ignore members they do not recognize, because a server may add members not defined in this specification. Servers should prefix added names with a short identifier and an underscore.

Servers may omit optional data according to their policies. The top-level rdapConformance array identifies specifications used to construct the response. The value rdap_level_0 identifies conformance with this specification; extensions use registered identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers can include extra fields, and clients should skip fields they do not understand. The response also names the specifications it follows.

sections.title: Common Data Types
sections.content:
The RFC sets formats for values used throughout RDAP. Handles are registry-unique identifiers. IPv4 addresses use dotted-decimal notation; IPv6 text follows RFC 5952. Country codes use the two-character alpha-2 form, while dates and times follow RFC 3339 and URIs follow RFC 3986.

DNS names may be LDH names, using letters, digits, and hyphens, or Unicode names containing at least one U-label. A trailing period is optional. Contact data uses jCard, the JSON form of vCard; its fn member is required and cannot be null.
sections.plainLanguage: The format specifies how to write common values such as addresses, dates, and country codes. This helps clients interpret the same value consistently.

sections.title: Shared Response Structures
sections.content:
Reusable structures include links, notices, remarks, language identifiers, events, statuses, public IDs, and object class names. Each response's top-level object must contain rdapConformance. Every response object must identify its class with objectClassName.

Links include required value, rel, and href members. Notices describe the service or whole response and appear only at the top level; remarks describe the object that contains them. Events include an action and date, and may identify an actor or include links.
sections.plainLanguage: Different record types reuse the same parts, such as links, notes, and event dates. Each record also says what kind of object it describes.

sections.title: The Five Registration Object Classes
sections.content:
RDAP defines five object classes. An entity represents a person, organization, or group and can include contact details in jCard. A nameserver can include LDH and Unicode names and IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. A domain includes its name, nameservers, related entities, variants, and optional DNSSEC data.

An IP network object records an address range and related registration details. An autnum object records an Autonomous System number or range; its start and end values are unsigned 32-bit integers. RIRs serve these last two classes; both RIRs and DNRs serve the first three.

Servers should provide a self link when possible. Clients must handle objects without one and should not cache a self link whose authority differs from the server that returned the data.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five record types for different kinds of registration: people or groups, nameservers, domains, IP networks, and AS numbers. Each type has fields suited to the information it describes.

sections.title: Errors, Searches, and Incomplete Results
sections.content:
An error response may include an errorCode matching the HTTP status, plus a title and description. A help response uses the notices structure. Search results contain arrays named for the searched object class, such as domainSearchResults, nameserverSearchResults, or entitySearchResults.

A truncated response remains valid JSON, but some search results or object data are missing. A server may explain this with a typed notice for a result set or a typed remark for an individual object.
sections.plainLanguage: Error responses can explain why a request failed. When an answer is incomplete, a notice or remark can tell the client that some data is missing.

sections.title: Security, Internationalization, and Privacy
sections.content:
Implementations should follow the JSON security guidance in RFC 8259 and the RDAP security guidance in RFCs 7480 and 7481. RDAP may return DNSSEC key data without the parent's signature, so that data is not generally trustworthy without additional information. Clients using self links for caches should guard against cache poisoning.

UTF-8 is the required default text encoding. Suggested status values can indicate private, removed, or obscured information. The RFC describes these as ways to signal that data is withheld or changed, not as a guarantee that a client will apply access controls.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP data still needs careful handling: JSON must be processed safely, and returned DNSSEC keys may need separate trust checks. Responses can also mark information that is private, removed, or altered.
